title: {{NAME}} and the Enchanted Final Whistle
moral: The bravest thing you can do is trust someone else when the moment matters most.

pages.content:
The Meadow of Ten Thousand Petals was the most extraordinary football pitch {{NAME}} had ever seen, and he had seen quite a few. The grass was the electric green of a traffic light, and it hummed softly underfoot. The goalposts were braided from living hawthorn branches, white blossoms trembling in an evening breeze that smelled faintly of warm honeycake.

How {{NAME}} had found it, he couldn't quite say. One moment he'd been chasing a runaway football through the hedge at the bottom of the park. The next, the hedge had simply opened, depositing him here, where the sky was a deep violet and the stars were already coming out, despite the fact that it was only half past four.

Tiny figures darted across the pitch. They were fairies, dozens of them, no taller than {{NAME}}'s forearm, wearing strips in every colour imaginable, chasing a ball that glowed like a captured moon.

pages.content:
The game stopped the moment the fairies noticed him. They landed in a ring around {{NAME}}, hovering at various heights, peering at him with large curious eyes the colours of jewels.

The captain stepped forward. She was taller than the rest, with wings the deep blue of a summer sky, and she wore a golden armband on her tiny arm with the authority of someone who had earned it. Her name was Fern, and she had a problem.

"We're one short," she said, looking {{NAME}} up and down as though measuring him for a suit of armour. "The Grand Solstice Match starts in ten minutes, and Dewdrop has twisted her wing." Behind her, a small fairy with gauzy white wings sat on a mushroom, looking dejected. "You're big, clumsy, and you've got enormous feet," Fern added, though not unkindly. "Can you play?"

{{NAME}} grinned. He had been playing since he could walk.

pages.content:
The opposition team, the Thornwing Fliers, were fast. Dizzyingly, furiously fast. They looped and spiralled and passed the glowing ball in arcs that no ordinary player could follow. {{NAME}} found himself sprinting, diving, sliding across the soft luminous grass, heart hammering, laughing despite himself.

His fairy teammates zipped around him in patterns they had clearly practised for centuries. Fern was everywhere at once, a blur of blue wings and fierce focus, calling out instructions in a language that {{NAME}} somehow understood perfectly in the heat of the game. Left! Through! OVER!

With two minutes left, the score was tied. {{NAME}} found the ball at his feet on the edge of the magical penalty arc, the glowing sphere pulsing against his orange boot. The Thornwing goalkeeper, a scarlet-winged fairy with eyes like chips of flint, crouched and narrowed her gaze.

Fern zipped to {{NAME}}'s side. She was unmarked on the left, completely open. She caught his eye and gave the smallest nod.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} could have shot. Every muscle in his leg wanted to shoot. The goal was right there, framed in hawthorn blossom, gleaming like a doorway to something wonderful.

But Fern was open. And Fern was faster, more precise, and had been playing this game since before the oldest oak tree in the park had been a seedling.

He passed.

The ball arced through the violet air in a long, clean, perfect curve. Fern's wings snapped wide. She met it at the peak of its flight, and with a crack that rang across the whole Meadow of Ten Thousand Petals, she struck it home.

The hawthorn goalposts erupted in blossom. White petals rained down like the world's smallest, most jubilant snowstorm. Every fairy in the meadow rose into the air at once, a constellation of wings catching starlight. Dewdrop, injured wing and all, leapt from her mushroom and spun in a tight joyful circle.

Fern landed in front of {{NAME}}. For the first time all evening, she smiled. It was a smile worth waiting for.

pages.content:
They celebrated long after the final whistle, dancing and spinning in the warm meadow air. Fern pressed a tiny acorn cup filled with something that tasted like honeyed starlight into {{NAME}}'s palm, and he drank it in one careful sip. It warmed him all the way to his toes.

The hedge was waiting for him when the violet sky began to shift toward indigo. Fern hovered at the gap. "You made the right choice," she said quietly, and {{NAME}} understood that she wasn't only talking about the pass.

He stepped through into the ordinary park. His football was waiting in the grass, still and round and perfectly normal. He tucked it under his arm and walked home through the long evening shadows, his orange boots still faintly warm with the memory of that glowing pitch.

Snuggled under his duvet, he turned the acorn cup over in his fingers and smiled. He was almost asleep when a thought floated through his mind like a leaf on water. What if, Fern had whispered at the very end, next time there are two matches?
